articles.title: Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave Is the Cure For a Terrible RPG Habit
articles.excerpt: Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave may let you recruit almost everyone on any route, but it's better to invest in a select few teammates
articles.body: For several hours, I spent my free time meandering the world map of Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave like a woman crazed. No matter what the calendar said, every day was Black Friday, and I was in feverish pursuit of gifts. From east to west and back again, I cleaned out vendors' stock of gifts for the several dozen randos I was determined to make my new besties. Back in Dagsion, I meticulously ticked through the full laundry list of recruitable characters and dutifully handed them their pastries or fish sauce, one swarthy pirate or pegasus girl blending into the next. I continued to do this for several in-game months, until I realized I wasn't actually enjoying the game to its fullest.

articles.title: AI Is Making Code Cheap. Verification Is Becoming the Expensive Part
articles.excerpt: Anthropic published a post about their CI infrastructure that I keep coming back to. The headline number is that Claude writes 80% of their code. That's the part everyone quoted. The part that stuck w…
articles.body: Anthropic published a post about their CI infrastructure that I keep coming back to. The headline number is that Claude writes 80% of their code. That's the part everyone quoted. The part that stuck with me was further down: their test suite grew 10x, and CI jobs went up 25x over six months. Read quickly, that's an infrastructure scaling story. Buy more compute, move on. I think it's something else. We spent years optimizing how fast developers could produce code, and AI is now removing that constraint faster than the systems around it can adapt. When code generation stops being the bottleneck, something else takes over. Going by Anthropic's numbers, that something is verification.

articles.title: The Leftover Hard Parts
articles.excerpt: Some time ago, I asked an AI to write a fairly boring piece of code. It did a pretty good job. I changed a few things, ran the tests, and voila: I was looking at something that probably would have tak…
articles.body: Some time ago, I asked an AI to write a fairly boring piece of code. It did a pretty good job. I changed a few things, ran the tests, and voila: I was looking at something that probably would have taken me most of the morning to write myself. This is the most exciting part of AI-assisted development for me: from idea to code in less than an hour. I felt great. Then a user hit a bug. They came back a second time, and something didn't work. The API needed to return something useful, but there wasn't an obvious answer. The generated code had handled the happy path perfectly well, but it had not really considered what should happen when the happy path wasn't happening. And why would it? I hadn't given it the answer. Someone had to decide what the product should actually do.

articles.title: Rust WebAssembly with WebForms Core 2.1
articles.excerpt: What is WebForms Core? WebForms Core is a modern multi-platform web technology from Elanat for building interactive HTML applications through server-defined commands and client-side command execution.…
articles.body: What is WebForms Core? WebForms Core is a modern multi-platform web technology from Elanat for building interactive HTML applications through server-defined commands and client-side command execution. WebForms Core uses a server-oriented architecture in which the server defines UI behavior through commands, while a lightweight browser runtime executes those commands. With WebForms Core 2.1 (WFC) , WebAssembly can also be used as an execution layer within this architecture. In this article, we will use Rust WebAssembly with WebForms Core and demonstrate two approaches: Rust with wasm-bindgen Raw WebAssembly using extern "C" Both approaches can execute Rust code through WebForms Core.

articles.title: I built an in-browser Swiss Army Knife with zero server uploads (PDFs, Images, JWT, Hashes)
articles.excerpt: Every day, developers and power users need quick micro-tasks done: Formatting or minifying a raw JSON response Inspecting a JWT header & checking expiration timestamps Stripping GPS coordinates and EX…
articles.body: Every day, developers and power users need quick micro-tasks done: Formatting or minifying a raw JSON response Inspecting a JWT header & checking expiration timestamps Stripping GPS coordinates and EXIF metadata from an image Converting a WebP/HEIC image to PNG Merging two PDF pages or rotating a document The problem? Most popular tools force you to upload sensitive company data, contracts, or auth tokens to third-party cloud servers. Plus, they hit you with daily limits or $15/month subscriptions. I built Convertum to solve this by bringing all processing 100% into the browser memory sandbox . 🛡️ Why Zero-Upload Matters When you paste an auth token into an online JWT inspector or upload an invoice to a cloud PDF merger, you're trusting an unknown backend with confidential data.

articles.body: 6 min read NASA-Funded Research Finds Complex Life Defying Record Heat This video shows Incendiamoeba cascadensis motility at 60ºC. When pushed to its limits in the lab, I. cascadensis can remain partially active at 150.8 degrees Fahrenheit (66 degrees Celsius) and can recover from exposure to a staggering 158 degrees Fahrenheit (70 degrees Celsius) for five minutes. However, 176 degrees Fahrenheit (80 degrees Celsius) proved to be too much for the amoeba to come back from. Beryl Rappaport Lee esta historia en español aquí . NASA-supported scientists have discovered an organism that lives at extreme temperatures previously thought impossible for complex life.
